t: Geometric Tolerance Checker - Signature build-tool concept
title: Geometric Tolerance Checker - Signature build-tool concept
definition: Evaluates models against specified geometric tolerances.
description:
Geometric Tolerance Checker is the Signature build-tool concept that evaluates models against specified geometric tolerances. In the Signature line, it is not a loose collection of scripts but a deterministic capability: the same build request produces the same verified result on every run, on every machine. This database documents the concept in full - what it is, the seven framework pillars that implement it, the real techniques it stands on, the standards it honors, and laddered drills that teach it from first principles to compounded mastery.

An AI that builds on demand needs Geometric Tolerance Checker the way a workshop needs its central bench. Without it, every build becomes improvisation: requirements drift, steps run out of order, and nobody can say why a result came out the way it did. With it, the build becomes a protocol - inputs declared, transformations explicit, outputs checked against the original request. That protocol is what these records describe, pillar by pillar.

Every record in this database carries a runnable demonstration program, because a build tool that cannot show its work cannot be trusted with real work. Read the overview, study the pillars, practice the drills, and run the demos: by the end the Geometric Tolerance Checker will be a capability you can invoke, not a concept you have read about.

t: Signature Sketcher - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
title: Signature Sketcher - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
definition: The Sketcher component of the Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework, owning sketcher. Signature concept.
description:
The Sketcher is a load-bearing component of the Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework. Its contract is narrow and absolute: within the framework, everything concerning the framework's sketcher responsibilities belongs to the Sketcher, and the Sketcher answers for it. This separation is what makes the framework testable - the Sketcher can be exercised alone, with declared inputs and checkable outputs, long before it is wired into a full build.

In operation the Sketcher works like this. A build request arrives carrying the Geometric Tolerance Checker charter (evaluates models against specified geometric tolerances.). The Sketcher reads its portion of the charter, performs its transformation, and hands a verified intermediate result to the next pillar. If its checks fail, it stops the line and reports exactly what was wrong, instead of passing corruption downstream. That fail-fast discipline is the Signature line's signature.

Signature-concept illustration: a builder asks for a small cad job that needs Geometric Tolerance Checker. The Sketcher takes the request's sketcher responsibilities slice, applies the framework's deterministic procedure, and returns its result with a proof of what it did. Run this record's demo program to see the Sketcher's core logic execute on a concrete example - the same logic, the same result, every run.

Signature framing: this pillar is part of the Signature line's original design for Geometric Tolerance Checker. It is labeled a Signature concept throughout - an engineered proposal, not an established public fact. The techniques it relies on are real and cited in the technique records of this database.

t: Signature Extruder - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
title: Signature Extruder - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
definition: The Extruder component of the Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework, owning extruder. Signature concept.
description:
Inside the Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework, the Extruder owns the framework's extruder responsibilities. Frameworks fail when responsibilities blur; the Signature line prevents that by giving each pillar a written contract, and the Extruder's contract is the sharpest of the seven. It accepts declared inputs, applies one deterministic transformation, and emits a result that any other pillar - or any auditor - can verify independently.

What distinguishes the Signature Extruder from an ad-hoc script is the verification loop. Every execution is checked against the charter (Evaluates models against specified geometric tolerances.). If the result cannot be justified against the charter, it is rejected and the build halts with a diagnostic instead of a silent wrong answer. Deterministic builds are not a slogan here; they are the acceptance test.

Same seed, same output: that reproducibility is the entire point.

t: Signature Filleter - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
title: Signature Filleter - Geometric Tolerance Checker framework pillar
definition: The Filleter component of the Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework, owning filleter. Signature concept.
description:
The Signature Geometric Tolerance Checker framework decomposes the capability (Evaluates models against specified geometric tolerances.) into seven pillars, and the Filleter is the one that owns the framework's filleter responsibilities. Owning a responsibility means three things in the Signature line: the pillar declares exactly what it accepts, it publishes exactly what it guarantees, and it logs enough evidence that a third party can replay its work and reach the same conclusion.

This discipline pays off when builds go wrong, because they always eventually do. When a Geometric Tolerance Checker result looks suspicious, the auditor does not re-run the whole build and hope; they replay the Filleter's log, check its guarantees against its inputs, and find the fault at its source. The pillar is thus both a worker and a witness - it does the work and it testifies about the work.

Try it yourself: this record's demo runs the Filleter's core procedure on a worked example. The program is plain JavaScript - save it as demo.js and run it with node, or press Run in the Demo Lab. Change the inputs and re-run; the procedure is deterministic, so you can verify every claim the description makes.
